title: If you feel no shame
hook: among the words of earlier prophecy: if you feel no shame, do as you wish (Nawawi 20, Abu Mas'ud)
tomorrow: a man wants one sentence he'll never need to ask about again. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday a boy heard: be mindful of Allah, he will protect you. The pages have dried. Today, a line the hadith says is older than that day.

A comment section at its worst has one thing in common: nobody posting seems embarrassed. Screenshots, pile-ons, a stranger's worst moment shared for a laugh. Al-Nawawi's twentieth hadith has a line for that. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it's among the words people have kept from earlier prophecy: if you feel no shame, do as you wish. So that's the line from earlier prophets. By the hadith's own account, it's older than the hadith. Handed down.
screen: `NOBODY SEEMS EMBARRASSED.` → `FROM EARLIER PROPHECY.` → `IF YOU FEEL NO SHAME…`

segments.voice: One question today: what keeps a person decent when nobody's checking? This hadith, from Sahih al-Bukhari, told by Abu Mas'ud, answers with haya: shame, modesty, the inner flinch before something low. 'Do as you wish' isn't permission. Read it as a warning, or as a description: once the flinch is gone, nothing inside is left to stop you. Not a law, not a fine, not a person watching: just the flinch, and it's gone. Another hadith calls haya a branch of faith. Shame guards. Now the thread to a neighbor. The hadith itself says the saying came from prophets before. The book of Jeremiah, read by Jews and Christians, grieves over a people who lost that same flinch: "Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush." Same alarm: the trouble isn't one wrong; it's a face that no longer blushes. And one honest difference. Jeremiah is a prophet grieving over his own people in his own time, a lament with a name and a place. The hadith carries the saying without naming which prophet first said it, and makes it a short rule anyone can pack. Two traditions, guarding the same door, ranked by no one. And haya isn't self-hatred. It's the guard at the door, not a prison.
screen: `HAYA: THE INNER FLINCH.` · `A WARNING, NOT A PERMISSION.` · `JEREMIAH: THEY COULD NOT BLUSH.` · `A GUARD, NOT A PRISON.` · then, large: `SHAME GUARDS.`

segments.voice: Pick up your phone and open the last thing you posted, sent, or almost sent. Look at it as if someone you deeply respect were reading over your shoulder. Don't delete anything; just notice whether there's a flinch, and where it sits. If there isn't one, that's fine too; you've just checked the lock.
If you feel no shame: a warning the hadith says came from earlier prophecy. Haya is the flinch that keeps you, even when no one is watching.
screen: `IF YOU FEEL NO SHAME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: shame guards. A blush isn't a failure; it's a lock that still works, on a door worth keeping. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1448 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY · 20 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN WANTS ONE SENTENCE HE'LL NEVER NEED TO ASK ABOUT AGAIN. WHAT?`

howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya as part of faith, in dress, speech and online life, and parents and teachers often quote 'if you feel no shame, do as you wish' as a gentle warning.
